label: Cold: hypothermia and frostbite
summary: Losing body heat faster than you make it leads to hypothermia, which kills, and frostbite, which kills skin and the tissue under it. Wind, wet clothes, too little food and water, and alcohol all speed it up. Poor judgement is an early sign, and people who are getting hypothermic may deny it.
signs: Early hypothermia: shivering, goose bumps, numb hands; a quick test is touching your thumb to your little finger
Getting worse: slow, clumsy movement, stumbling, slurred speech, poor judgement, confusion, drowsiness
Severe: shivering weakens or stops, then the person becomes unresponsive and breathing slows
Frostnip: skin turns pale, yellowish or white but is still soft underneath
Frostbite: numb, waxy, hard and colder than the skin around it; later blisters, swelling, a dull purple colour, or black skin
Wind chill of −28 to −39: exposed skin can freeze in 10–30 minutes; −40 to −47, in 5–10; −48 to −54, in 2–5; −55 or colder, in under 2. In sustained winds over 50 km/h, faster still
do: Dress in loose layers with a windproof outer layer, wool or synthetics next to the skin rather than cotton, and a hat. Wear mittens below about −17 °C
Stay dry: take layers off before you sweat, and change out of wet clothing as soon as you can
Eat and drink regularly, take warm-up breaks in shelter, and work in pairs, checking each other's face, ears, nose and fingers for numbness or white patches
Insulate metal tool handles, and wear gloves to handle metal and fuel
If skin freezes to metal, free it by warming the spot with warm water (or urine) instead of pulling
Stranded in a vehicle: stay with it unless help is very close, bundle up, keep moving your arms and legs, take turns sleeping, and see Carbon monoxide before running the engine for heat
dont: Don't touch cold metal with bare or wet hands: skin freezes to it and tears off
Don't get fuel, antifreeze or oil on your skin in the cold: cooled liquids can cause frostbite
Don't drink alcohol to warm up: it makes you feel warm while you lose heat faster
Don't rub frostbite or rub snow on it, and don't warm it at a fire, stove, heater or exhaust: numb skin burns without you feeling it
Don't thaw a frozen hand or foot if it might freeze again before you reach shelter, and avoid walking on a thawed foot
Don't wear tight boots, gloves or clothing: they cut off blood flow
ppe: Loose layers you can open and shed, a waterproof and windproof outer layer, a warm hat covering the ears, a face mask in cold wind, mittens, and wool socks with a spare pair
Down keeps you warm only while dry; it loses almost all its warmth when wet
Insulated boots. In safety boots, makers say composite toe caps don't conduct cold the way steel ones do
firstAid: Hypothermia: get them out of wind and wet, take off wet clothing, wrap them in dry layers or a sleeping bag with head and neck covered, handle them gently and let them lie down rather than stand or walk

Warm the trunk, not the limbs: warm (not hot) bottles or packs wrapped in cloth on the chest and upper body, or skin-to-skin in a sleeping bag. Don't rub arms and legs, use a heat lamp or put them in a hot bath
Warm, sweet drinks only if they are alert enough to swallow safely; nothing if drowsy, unconscious or fitting
Not breathing: start CPR and keep going. People this cold who seemed dead have been revived

Frostbite that can stay thawed: soak it in water at 37–39 °C (warm but bearable on a helper's uninjured hand for 30 seconds) for about 30 minutes. Pat dry, leave blisters alone, wrap loosely in dry dressings and raise it above the heart
